By the three-perpendiculars theorem, the foot $H$ of the altitude from $A$ to plane $BCD$ projects orthogonally onto $BC$ at the same point $F$ as the altitude of $\triangle ABC$, and onto $BD$ at the same point $G$ as the altitude of $\triangle ABD$. Hence $HF\perp BC$ and $HG\perp BD$, so the two constructed perpendiculars in the base plane indeed locate $H$. Since $AH\perp BH$, the right triangle with hypotenuse $AB$ and leg $BH$ has remaining leg $AH=\sqrt{AB^2-BH^2}$, which is constructible with straightedge and compass and equals the required altitude. All six given edges are used: $BC,BD,CD$ for the base, $AB,AC$ for $\triangle ABC$, and $AB,AD$ for $\triangle ABD$.

In the plane of }\triangle BCD\text{ draw the line through }M\text{ perpendicular to }BC\text{ and the line through }N\text{ perpendicular to }BD;\text{ let }H\text{ be their intersection.}\\ \text{5. **Derivation.** Let \(H\) be the orthogonal projection of \(A\) onto the plane \(BCD\). In face \(ABC\), the altitude from \(A\) to \(BC\) meets \(BC\) at a point \(M\) with \(AM\perp BC\). Orthogonal projection onto the plane \(BCD\) fixes \(BC\) and sends \(A\) to \(H\), so it sends \(AM\) to \(HM\); since projection preserves orthogonality to lines lying in the plane, \(HM\perp BC\). Thus \(H\) lies on the perpendicular to \(BC\) through \(M\). The same reasoning applied to face \(BD\) shows \(H\) lies on the perpendicular to \(BD\) through \(N\). Hence \(H\) is the intersection constructed in step 4. Finally, in right triangle \(AHB\) we have \(AH^2=AB^2-BH^2\), so step 5 produces a segment equal to the altitude from \(A\). All steps use only straight-edge and compass.

\boxed{\text{Construct }\triangle BCD\text{ with sides }S_4,S_5,S_6,\text{ its area }S,\text{ the volume }V\text{ via the Cayley--Menger determinant, then }h_A=3V/S.}

**Derivation.**  
1. By SSS, construct $\triangle BCD$ in the plane from the given segments $S_4=BC$, $S_5=BD$, $S_6=CD$.  
2. Its area $S=[BCD]$ is constructible: Heron's formula expresses $S$ using only rational operations and square roots of the side lengths, all of which are straightedge–compass constructible.  
3. The Cayley–Menger determinant gives $288V^2$ as a polynomial with integer coefficients in the six squared edge lengths $S_1^2,\dots,S_6^2$. Hence $V$ is obtained from the given lengths by a finite sequence of additions, multiplications, divisions and one extraction of a square root, so $V$ (and therefore $3V$) is constructible.  
4. The altitude from $A$ to face $BCD$ satisfies $V=\frac13 S\cdot h_A$, i.e. $h_A=3V/S$. Given constructible lengths $3V$ and $S$, the quotient is constructed as a fourth proportional by similar triangles.  
5. Because the six segments come from a non-degenerate tetrahedron, $S>0$ and $V>0$, so $h_A$ is a well-defined positive length. Every step uses only straightedge and compass, producing a segment congruent to the desired altitude.

Let $H$ be the orthogonal projection of $A$ onto plane $BCD$. Then $AB^{2}-BH^{2}=AC^{2}-CH^{2}=AD^{2}-DH^{2}=h^{2}$, so $BH^{2}-CH^{2}=S_{1}^{2}-S_{2}^{2}$.  
In the plane, the locus $\{X:XB^{2}-XC^{2}=S_{1}^{2}-S_{2}^{2}\}$ is the line through $P$ perpendicular to $BC$, where $P$ is the foot of the altitude in the planar triangle $ABC(S_{1},S_{2},S_{4})$, because $PB^{2}-PC^{2}=AB^{2}-AC^{2}$.  
Similarly, using triangle $ABD(S_{1},S_{3},S_{5})$ on $BD$, $H$ lies on the line through $Q$ perpendicular to $BD$.  
These two perpendiculars meet at the unique point $H$ (strict tetrahedron inequalities prevent degeneracy).  
Finally $h=\sqrt{S_{1}^{2}-BH^{2}}$ is obtained as the leg of a right triangle with hypotenuse $S_{1}$ and other leg $BH$.  
Every step uses only straightedge and compass (copying segments, erecting perpendiculars, intersections); $H$ may lie outside $\triangle BCD$, which causes no difficulty.
